audit_status.source_base: Hebrew 2 Kings / Melakhim Bet Joash reign, temple-repair finance, Hazael tribute, and assassination narrative, draft aligned later
audit_status.review_note: First-pass draft reviewed for child-king maturation under Jehoiada, high-place continuity, dedicated-money categories, failed repair system, chest collection, counting and distribution controls, artisan trust, priestly revenue, imperial tribute from sacred treasury, and palace assassination.

verses.restored: In seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash became king, and forty years he reigned in Jerusalem. Name of his mother was Zibiah from Beer-sheba.
Jehoash did what was right in eyes of YHWH all his days in which Jehoiada the priest instructed him.
Only high places were not removed; people were still sacrificing and burning incense at high places.

Jehoash said to priests, All silver of sacred gifts brought into house of YHWH—the silver of each one who passes assessment, silver of persons according to valuation, and all silver that comes upon a person's heart to bring into house of YHWH—
let priests take it, each from his acquaintance, and let them repair breaches of house wherever a breach is found.
But in twenty-third year of king Jehoash, priests had not repaired breaches of house.
King Jehoash called Jehoiada the priest and other priests and said, Why are you not repairing breaches of house? Now take no more silver from your acquaintances, but give it for breaches of house.
Priests consented not to take silver from people and not to repair breaches of house.

Jehoiada the priest took one chest, bored a hole in its lid, and placed it beside altar, on right as one enters house of YHWH. Priests guarding threshold put there all silver brought into house of YHWH.
Whenever they saw much silver in chest, scribe of king and high priest came up, bound and counted silver found in house of YHWH.
They gave counted silver into hands of those doing work, those appointed over house of YHWH, and they paid it to carpenters and builders working on house of YHWH,
to masons and stonecutters, to buy timber and hewn stone to repair breaches of house of YHWH, and for all spent on house to repair it.
Yet no silver basins, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, any vessel of gold or vessel of silver were made for house of YHWH from silver brought into house of YHWH,
for they gave it to workers and repaired house of YHWH with it.
They did not make accounting with men into whose hands they gave silver to give to workers, because they dealt faithfully.
Silver of guilt offerings and silver of sin offerings was not brought into house of YHWH; it belonged to priests.
Then Hazael king of Aram went up, fought against Gath, and captured it. Hazael set his face to go up against Jerusalem.

Jehoash king of Judah took all sacred gifts Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah his fathers, kings of Judah, had dedicated, his own sacred gifts, and all gold found in treasuries of house of YHWH and king's house, and sent it to Hazael king of Aram. Then he went away from Jerusalem.
Remaining acts of Joash and all he did, are they not written in scroll of matters of days of kings of Judah?
His servants rose and made a conspiracy, and struck Joash at house of Millo, on way descending to Silla.
Jozacar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer, his servants, struck him, and he died. They buried him with his fathers in city of David, and Amaziah his son became king in his place.

translation_notes: Joash begins as a rescued child and rules under Jehoiada's instruction. His later authority does not erase the formative control adults exercised around him.

Temple-repair money initially passes through informal priestly relationships, and the repairs remain undone for decades. Sacred status does not remove the need for transparent systems and measurable outcomes.
The chest, joint counting by royal and priestly officials, and direct payment to supervisors and artisans show financial controls replacing an ineffective arrangement.
Trust in work supervisors is praised, but this verse must not be used to reject audits, worker protections, receipts, or modern fiduciary accountability.
Carpenters, builders, masons, stonecutters, and suppliers perform the repair. Their labor, skill, safety, and fair payment belong at the center of the temple story.

Sacred and royal treasures are transferred to Hazael to avert attack. A ruler's survival strategy can preserve a city while also exposing dependence, extortion, and the vulnerability of public resources.
Joash is assassinated by servants. The narrative provides no trial or full motive here; conspiracy and regicide are not accountability systems.
Parallel material in Chronicles differs substantially and requires source-witness audit rather than forced harmonization.
safety_note: Do not use this chapter to excuse clerical financial opacity, unpaid sacred labor, imperial extortion, or assassination. Preserve transparent stewardship, skilled workers' dignity, public accountability, and the distinction between protecting a community and buying a ruler's security with communal treasure.
